headline: Strength is a [[vital sign.]]
body: Why muscle function belongs at the centre of GLP-1 care.

headline: Weaker grip, [[higher risk.]]
body: Across 139,691 adults in 17 countries, every 5 kg lower grip strength carried a 16% higher risk of death from any cause.

headline: It outranked [[blood pressure.]]
body: In the same study, grip strength predicted all-cause and cardiovascular death more strongly than systolic blood pressure.

headline: Sarcopenia starts with [[low strength.]]
body: The revised European consensus makes low muscle strength the key sign of sarcopenia, confirmed by low muscle quantity or quality.

headline: Excess weight can [[hide weak muscle.]]
body: ESPEN and EASO define sarcopenic obesity as excess fat with low muscle mass and function, and advise assessing muscle function first.

headline: Training [[moves the needle.]]
body: Across 73 trials and 3,059 older adults, progressive resistance training had a large effect on strength and made rising from a chair easier.
source: Liu and Latham, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2009

name: Prof. Stuart Gray
role: Professor of Muscle and Metabolic Health, University of Glasgow
points: Research: sarcopenia, resistance exercise and nutrition

headline: How we build [[strength into care.]]
items: Physician-supervised GLP-1 therapy, metabolic panel at each MD consult
Coached training once or twice a week toward 150 minutes
Custom meal plan and monthly protein supply
Body composition logged and shared with each patient
Physician-guided tapering and a maintenance phase
Grip strength tracks with mortality risk.
Low strength is the key sign of sarcopenia.
Obesity can mask low muscle function.
